Bybit vs Binance

A no-nonsense side-by-side of Bybit and Binance for crypto futures — leverage, fees, maintenance margin and what each is actually good at. Whichever you pick, plan the trade first with our free calculators.

TL;DR — our verdict

Pick Bybit if you want a fast matching engine and deep USDT-perpetual liquidity. Pick Binance if the largest volume and the widest range of futures pairs matters more. Binance is cheaper on base taker fees; Binance has the higher leverage cap. Not sure yet? Practice the strategy free before funding either.

Which should you pick?

If you want a fast matching engine and deep USDT-perpetual liquidity, go with Bybit. If the largest volume and the widest range of futures pairs matters more, Binance fits better. Many traders keep accounts on both and route each trade to wherever the liquidity and funding are best on the day. There is no wrong answer — there is only an unplanned trade.

What the fees actually cost you

This is the one pairing on this site where the fee gap is large enough to decide the question on its own. Binance charges 0.04% against Bybit's 0.055%, and because the fee lands on notional — the whole leveraged position, not the margin behind it — and is paid entering and exiting, the difference compounds fast:

 BybitBinance
Taker per side0.055%0.04%
Round-trip cost$11.00$8.00
Over 100 trades$1,100.00$800.00

Over a hundred round trips that is $300.00 in Binance's favour — enough to notice on a small account. Keep it in proportion though: one liquidation you could have avoided costs more than a year of the difference. Both venues price maker orders below taker and cut rates as 30-day volume grows. Model it against your own size with the funding-fee calculator and the PnL calculator.

Leverage: what the caps really mean here

Binance advertises 125x against Bybit's 100x. Read that as a ceiling, not a recommendation: at 125x a move of about 0.80% against the position is enough to end it, against 1.00% at the lower cap. Traders who survive rarely trade anywhere near either number, so a higher cap is only an advantage if you already know why you need it.

Which venue is actually blowing traders up right now

A venue carrying a bigger share of the day's liquidations is not automatically the riskier place to trade — it usually means more leveraged size is open there. The full nine-venue breakdown, updated continuously, sits on the liquidation feed, and the same numbers are free as JSON at /api/v1/venues.

Safety, regulation & track record

Both opened within 1 year of each other (Bybit 2018, Binance 2017), so neither wins on track record alone.

Bybit publishes proof-of-reserves and has no major custodial hack on record; restricted in several regulated markets and not open to US residents. Binance the largest venue by volume, publishes proof-of-reserves, and now operates under tighter compliance after its 2023 US settlement; futures are not available to US residents.

Neither is available to US residents — a US-regulated venue such as Kraken fits that case better. Whichever you choose, never keep more on any exchange than you are actively trading, enable withdrawal whitelists and two-factor authentication, and confirm current fees, leverage caps and regional availability on the exchange itself before funding.
